extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (public relations managers, PR departments, agency staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and evaluating organizational public relations communications (press releases, publicity, promotional materials) with emphasis on legal compliance, evaluation research, media access, and ethical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for research and statistical skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners must know basic research methods: sampling theory, questionnaire construction, and basic statistics to do evaluation research or work with researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want to do your own research or become a full-time researcher, learn sampling theory, questionnaire construction, and basic statistics. Courses in research methods and statistics are recommended because research is a day-to-day component of public relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the organization’s right to communicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations, including corporations, enjoy First Amendment protections and can participate in the free exchange of ideas; courts have extended many speech protections to organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the legal articulation of rights to speak and to be heard, historical court positions, and the distinction between organizational speech and individual speech when planning communications or engaging in public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comply with broadcast rules (Fairness Doctrine & personal-attack rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasters have obligations under the FCC’s Fairness Doctrine to devote reasonable air time to public issues and present opposing viewpoints; the FCC’s personal-attack rule requires notifying attacked persons and affording a reasonable opportunity to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When communicating via broadcast media, expect requirements to provide balancing viewpoints and to run replies at comparable times and reach. Replies need not be free if the original broadcast was a paid announcement. Familiarity with FCC regulations and interpretations can create opportunities and avoid liabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use FOIA to get government-held information properly
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the U.S. Freedom of Information Act, 'any person' (including corporations) has a right to access agency records except those covered by nine exemptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FOI requests must 'reasonably describe' desired records; requesters needn't state a reason but doing so may hasten searches. Be aware of exemptions (national security, trade secrets, privacy) and that fees are limited to 'reasonable standard charges.' Keep up with changing interpretations and procedural rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid libel and slander (defamation) in releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Libel (written) and slander (spoken) are defamation—an utterance tending to impugn honesty, character, or reputation—and false derogatory statements that injure professional standing can lead to suits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise care in justifying personnel actions or criticizing others. Retractions and/or apologies can reduce damages. Beware of punitive damages when malice or 'reckless disregard for the truth' can be shown. Consider community values and the possibility that the same words may be judged differently in different settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for public-figure/actual-malice standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary about 'public' persons is broadly protected, but public officials/figures must prove 'actual malice'—that the statement was made with knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth—to recover damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When communicating about public figures, understand that courts give wider leeway to commentary but that 'actual malice' is the standard for defamation claims involving public officials or public figures; craft statements accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain photographic and image releases for promotional use
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations departments should obtain signed release forms from identifiable persons in photographs intended for publicity or promotional use; for minors obtain parental/guardian signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a simple photographic release form (sample provided) that describes the photograph, grants permission for publicity/promotional purposes, and waives claims for compensation. If payment is made, the release should state the consideration. Do not assume presence in a group photo constitutes permission for promotional use—distinguish news use from promotional use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect copyright—ascertain ownership and obtain permission
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume broad usage equals public domain. Copyright protects literary and artistic property and permission (and sometimes payment) is required to appropriate others' material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always determine who owns rights to material and obtain permission before using it. Consider 'work made for hire' rules (ownership and terms differ), and remember that statutory protection exists for unpublished works. Registration procedures are available from the Copyright Office. Even tiny excerpts (e.g., two lines of a song) may be protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the fair use factors when claiming fair use
rubrics_metrics.description: Fair use depends on (1) purpose and character of the use; (2) nature of the copyrighted work; (3) amount used in relation to the whole work; and (4) effect on the potential market for the copyrighted work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate these four factors before claiming fair use. Use for commentary, education, or minimal excerpting may favor fair use, but promotional/commercial reuse is less likely to be covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious using 'works made for hire' and understand ownership/term
rubrics_metrics.description: Works produced by employees or by contract may be 'works made for hire' and subject to different copyright ownership and longer protection terms (e.g., 75 years from publication under discussed rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify in advance who owns copyright when employees or outside writers produce materials, especially if individuals sometimes publish separately. Understand the copyright term implications for company-owned works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect privacy rights (intrusion, misappropriation, false light, private facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals are protected from intrusion, misappropriation of name/likeness, publicity placing them in false light, and disclosure of private embarrassing facts; privacy law balances personal privacy and information gathering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a person is a 'public figure' (reduced privacy protections). Obtain permission for use of images/descriptions in promotional materials. Distinguish news reporting from promotional use—promotional use usually requires releases. Exercise care using employee photos and 'real people' endorsements; review legal guidance on publicity and privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish news coverage from promotional use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of images or information in a legitimate news context may be permissible without a release, while promotional or advertisement use typically requires permission and/or payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt (e.g., group tours where promotional emphasis is later added), secure releases—particularly for minors or when the use goes beyond internal corporate communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid speculative or misleading financial publicity (SEC constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC bans many promotional activities concerning securities, including optimistic sales/earnings projections based on 'wishful thinking,' glowing descriptions of experimental products, vague merger announcements, undue stress on favorable news, leaking rumors, and favoring analysts with undisclosed material news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not release speculative information that could affect stock prices. Comply with SEC rules on material disclosure and avoid selective disclosure to favored analysts. Use caution in financial PR to avoid SEC enforcement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'issuance of prospectus' in improper form—observe quiet periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity that effectively constitutes an offering (a 'prospectus') but is not in the legally required form violates securities law; during the registration/quiet period certain information and promotional activities are prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not issue promotional materials about a securities offering outside proper prospectus forms. Recognize the 'quiet period' rules and restrict communications that could be construed as offering securities before registration is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comply with SEC reporting requirements (Form 10-K, quarterly reports) and timely disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies must prepare an annual report using SEC Form 10-K within specified deadlines and follow complex rules for interim quarterly reports; the SEC seeks 'continuous disclosure' of material financial information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations must coordinate with finance/legal to prepare required disclosures timely and accurately. Anticipate expanded disclosure requirements (discussion of unfavorable trends, methods behind sales predictions, departmental details) that may reduce marketing spin in required filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selective disclosure and leaks of material nonpublic information
rubrics_metrics.description: Favoring certain analysts or releasing undisclosed material information to a select audience is prohibited and can have legal consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure material information is made broadly public per legal/regulatory expectations rather than selectively communicated; implement policies and training to prevent unauthorized leaks and rumor creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comply with advertising regulation and consumer-protection measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Government agencies (e.g., FTC, FCC) regulate advertising and commercial speech; some limitations exist though courts have sometimes extended First Amendment protection to commercial speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid false or misleading advertising claims. Monitor agency rulings and regulations relevant to commercial communications and ensure PR materials conform to advertising laws and consumer-protection standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider legal constraints affecting lobbying, employees, and foreign agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws affect what organizations may communicate regarding employees, lobbying activities, and representation of foreign interests (e.g., laws affecting lobbyists and foreign agents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations managers must be aware of the legal environment for lobbying disclosures, employee communications, and foreign agent registration/limitations; consult legal counsel when planning related communications.
